title: PESTLE & SWOT: what shapes the business case
blurb: Use PESTLE and SWOT to find the factors that influence a project's business case, and know which are internal and which are external.
question: A regional bus company is preparing a business case to replace its diesel fleet with electric buses. A government grant is available, electricity prices are unpredictable and the company has no electric-bus maintenance skills. How would PESTLE and SWOT help the team find and use these factors?

teach.h: Reading the world around the project
teach.body: A business case justifies a project by weighing its benefits against its costs and risks. All three depend on factors the project does not control: government policy, prices, laws, competitors, and the organisation's own skills and resources. PESTLE and SWOT are tools for finding those factors early. PESTLE scans the external environment; SWOT sets the organisation's internal strengths and weaknesses against external opportunities and threats.

letters.sub: Inflation, interest and exchange rates, demand
Laws and regulations: employment, data, safety

teach.caption: Two Es: Economic comes second, Environmental comes last. Every PESTLE factor is EXTERNAL to the organisation.
Top row: things the organisation controls. Bottom row: things happening outside it.

teach.h: How the findings shape the business case
teach.body: These tools are only useful if their findings change decisions. External factors and threats become risks to manage, or reasons to rule options out. Opportunities can enlarge benefits or reduce costs. Weaknesses show what the project must fix or buy in. Economic and legal findings change cost estimates and timescales. Anything uncertain becomes a recorded assumption to watch, because if it changes, the business case may no longer hold.

teach.h: Valley Buses' SWOT, and what it changes
teach.body: Strengths: depots with space for chargers and a trusted local brand. Weaknesses: no electric-bus maintenance skills and an ageing scheduling system. Opportunities: the government grant and an energy firm keen to partner. Threats: long supplier lead times and a rival bidding for the same routes. So the business case adds a training work package (weakness), times the bid to secure the grant (opportunity) and orders early with contingency (threat).

teach.h: A typical way to use them together

steps.label: Build the SWOT
steps.sub: Sort into S, W, O and T

teach.caption: Linear: done in Concept and re-checked at each decision gate. Iterative: done in Feasibility and Foundations, then revisited as priorities are reset between iterations.

rows.label: Feeds
values: SWOT's O and T, risks, assumptions

teach.text: Classic trap: mixing up the SWOT rows. Strengths and Weaknesses are INTERNAL; Opportunities and Threats are EXTERNAL. A new law, a rival firm or bad weather is a threat, never a weakness, because the organisation does not control it. In PESTLE, 'L' is Legal (not Leadership) and there are two Es: Economic and Environmental.

teach.h: How this comes up in a written answer
items: Name the tool and its purpose: PESTLE scans the external environment; SWOT sets internal strengths and weaknesses against external opportunities and threats.
Give real examples under the headings, tied to the scenario in the question.
Explain how each finding influences the business case: options, risks, benefits, costs or timescales.
Say how the organisation would respond: exploit strengths and opportunities, address weaknesses, manage threats.
Note that the analysis is revisited, because the environment changes.
PESTLE: Political, Economic, Social, Technological, Legal, Environmental: all external.
SWOT: Strengths and Weaknesses are internal; Opportunities and Threats are external.
Findings feed the business case: options, risks, benefits, costs and assumptions.
Threats become risks to manage; weaknesses become work to fix or skills to buy in.
Revisit the analysis at decision gates or between iterations as things change.

summary: You can now list the six PESTLE headings and the four SWOT elements, classify a factor as internal or external, and explain how the findings shape a business case's options, risks, benefits and costs. You also know to revisit the analysis as the environment changes.

A.q: In PESTLE analysis, what does the 'L' stand for?
A.why: L is Legal: laws and regulations such as employment, health and safety, and data protection.

whyNot.1: Leadership is an internal matter; PESTLE only covers the external environment.
whyNot.2: Logistics is an operational concern, not a PESTLE heading.
whyNot.3: Labour market conditions fall under Economic or Social, not a separate L.

A.q: Which elements of a SWOT analysis describe factors INTERNAL to the organisation?
A.why: Strengths and weaknesses are internal: the organisation's own capabilities, resources and limitations.

whyNot.0: Opportunities and threats are both external.
whyNot.1: Strengths are internal, but threats are external.
whyNot.3: Weaknesses are internal, but opportunities are external.

A.q: A project team wants a structured scan of the wider external environment before drafting a business case. Which tool is MOST suitable?
A.why: PESTLE gives a structured scan of the external environment under six headings.

whyNot.0: A RACI chart allocates responsibilities for work.
whyNot.2: A Gantt chart shows a schedule over time.
whyNot.3: A resource histogram shows resource demand over time.

B.q: During a PESTLE review for a new data centre, the team notes that new data protection rules will require extra security controls. Under which PESTLE heading does this BEST belong?
B.why: Data protection rules are law and regulation, so they belong under Legal.

whyNot.0: Political covers government policy and stability; the rules themselves are legal requirements.
whyNot.1: The security controls are technical, but the driver here is a legal requirement.
whyNot.2: Social covers attitudes and demographics, not regulation.

B.q: Valley Buses finds it has no in-house skills to maintain electric buses. In its SWOT analysis, this is BEST classed as a:
options: Threat, as it could delay the project
Weakness, as it is an internal gap
Strength, as the gap is known early
B.why: A lack of in-house skills is an internal limitation, which makes it a weakness.

whyNot.0: Threats are external. The skills gap is inside the organisation, even though it could cause delay.
whyNot.2: Opportunities are external chances; recruiting is a response to the weakness.
whyNot.3: Knowing about a gap does not turn it into a strength.

B.q: How do PESTLE and SWOT findings MOST directly help a business case?
options: They reveal factors shaping options and risks
They replace the need for a cost-benefit appraisal
They fix the project scope so it cannot change
They show the schedule's critical path and float
B.why: Both tools surface factors that influence and impact the business case: which options are viable, the risks, and the size and timing of costs and benefits.

whyNot.1: They inform the appraisal; they do not replace weighing costs against benefits.
whyNot.2: They do not fix scope. If anything, they show where the case may need to change.
whyNot.3: Critical path and float come from network scheduling, not environmental analysis.

C.q:
A hotel group's SWOT for a new spa lists:
1) Strong brand: Strength
2) Ageing booking system: Weakness
3) High staff turnover: Threat
4) Growing wellness market: Opportunity
Which item is in the WRONG box?
C.why: High staff turnover is an internal problem the hotel can act on, so it is a weakness, not a threat.

whyNot.0: A strong brand is an internal advantage: a strength.
whyNot.1: An ageing internal system is a weakness.
whyNot.3: A growing market is an external chance: an opportunity.

C.q: Which of the following is NOT a typical way PESTLE findings feed into a business case?
options: Identifying external risks to the benefits
Ruling out options that break the law
Allocating work packages to the team
C.why: Allocating work packages is detailed resource planning, done later with the WBS and OBS. It is not a use of PESTLE.

whyNot.0: External factors often become risks to the project's benefits.
whyNot.1: Economic findings test cost assumptions such as inflation or energy prices.
whyNot.2: Legal findings can rule out options that would not comply.

C.q: Valley Buses' business case was approved a year ago. A PESTLE refresh now shows the government grant has been withdrawn. What is the MOST appropriate response?
options: Ignore it, as the case is already approved
Move the grant into the SWOT strengths
Wait to report it in the closure report
C.why: A major external change can undermine the justification, so the business case should be reassessed and the sponsor decide whether to continue, change or stop.

whyNot.0: Approval is not permanent; the business case must stay valid throughout.
whyNot.2: A grant is external, and losing it is a threat, not a strength.
whyNot.3: Waiting until closure means spending more without knowing the case still holds.

reteach.title: Planning a summer music festival
reteach.question: A team is planning a first summer festival in a town park. Before booking any bands, they ask what is happening in the world around them, and what they are good and bad at. How do PESTLE and SWOT help?

blocks.body: PESTLE looks outward. Political: the council's licensing policy. Economic: can families afford tickets this year? Social: demand for family-friendly events. Technological: cashless payment at bars. Legal: noise and licensing laws. Environmental: weather, litter and the park's wildlife. SWOT then adds the inside view: what the team itself is good and bad at, set against those outside chances and dangers.

blocks.text: Rain on the day is not a weakness. The team cannot control the weather, so it is an external threat (and an Environmental factor in PESTLE).

explain.body: Political, Economic, Social, Technological, Legal, Environmental. Each prompts the team to look at one part of the external environment so nothing important is missed.

test.q: Rising interest rates that increase the cost of borrowing for a project belong under which PESTLE heading?
test.why: Interest rates, inflation and exchange rates are Economic factors.

whyNot.1: Political covers government policy and stability, not market interest rates.
whyNot.3: Environmental covers climate, emissions and natural surroundings.

explain.body: Strengths and weaknesses are inside the organisation, so it can change them. Opportunities and threats come from outside, so it can only respond to them.

test.q: A competitor is about to launch a rival product. In a SWOT analysis, this is BEST classed as a:
test.why: A competitor's action is external and potentially harmful: a threat.

whyNot.0: Weaknesses are internal shortcomings; the competitor is outside the organisation.
whyNot.3: A rival launch is harmful rather than a chance to exploit.

explain.body: Use strengths to seize opportunities. Fix or buy in what weaknesses lack. Plan responses to threats. Those actions shape the project's options, scope, risks and costs in the business case.

test.q: Valley Buses owns depots with space for chargers, and a government grant is available. What does SWOT suggest it should do?
options: Treat the depots as a risk to be avoided
Log both items as threats in the register
Ignore them until delivery has started
Use the strength to seize the opportunity
test.why: Matching an internal strength (depot space) to an external opportunity (the grant) is the most valuable use of a SWOT.

whyNot.0: The depots are a strength, not a risk.
whyNot.1: Neither is a threat: one is a strength and one an opportunity.
whyNot.2: Ignoring them wastes the chance to shape a stronger business case.

explain.body: The environment moves: grants end, prices swing, laws change. Re-run the analysis at decision gates in a linear life cycle, or when priorities are reset between iterations, and check the business case still holds.

test.q: When should PESTLE and SWOT findings be revisited?
options: Only once, before the project starts
At reviews such as decision gates
Only after the project has closed
Only when the sponsor is replaced
test.why: The environment changes, so findings should be refreshed at reviews such as decision gates to check the business case is still valid.

whyNot.0: A single analysis goes out of date as the environment changes.
whyNot.2: After closure it is too late to protect the investment.
whyNot.3: A change of sponsor is not the only trigger; the environment can change at any time.
